query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A rapid cooling treatment immediately after casting, followed by an optimized annealing schedule, refines the lamellar microstructure in eutectic high-entropy alloys, which simultaneously increases both strength and ductility compared to conventional slow-cooled and non-optimized annealed samples.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) produced by standard casting with a coarse lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
generation.intervention: Rapid cooling (high cooling rate) immediately after casting followed by a controlled, short-duration annealing cycle at an optimized temperature.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be applied under ambient conditions and be benchmarked against the conventional processing route; it applies to eutectic HEAs where a dual-phase lamellar microstructure is present.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined lamellar spacing and improved phase morphology at the fcc/B2 interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The rapid cooling suppresses excessive coarsening by freezing a fine-scale lamellar arrangement, while the subsequent controlled annealing relieves internal stresses and slightly coarsens the most critical interfaces. This refined microstructure enhances strength via increased interface density and improves ductility by facilitating more uniform plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloys will exhibit a higher yield and ultimate tensile strength (improved by an estimated ~15-25% relative to conventional processing) along with improved ductility (e.g., elongation increase by a comparable percentage), relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic HEAs produced via slow cooling and standard annealing, which yield a coarser lamellar structure with lower strength and ductility.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected only in eutectic HEAs with a well-defined lamellar microstructure; alloys lacking distinct dual-phase structures or those that are prone to deleterious phase transformations under rapid cooling might not exhibit the improvement.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from similar thermomechanical treatments in eutectic HEAs supports the refinement of lamellar microstructures, the exact processing parameters (cooling rate, annealing time/temperature) yielding the optimal strength-ductility balance require further calibration, and quantitative improvements may vary with alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set processed via conventional slow cooling and standard annealing (baseline) and the other using the rapid cooling plus optimized annealing schedule. Characterize the microstructure for lamellar refinement using electron microscopy and measure mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation via tensile tests).
measurements: Lamellar spacing and phase distribution (using SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the rapid cooling plus annealing treatment does not result in statistically significant simultaneous improvements in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the conventional baseline, or if the microstructure does not show a refined lamellar arrangement, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al. [,] designed the CoCrFeNiNbx EHEAs and found that the microstructures were stable from 600 °C to 900 °C.

occupying_moves.technique: controlled heat-treatment experiments (rapid solidification followed by tailored annealing)
occupying_moves.conditions: tested on eutectic high-entropy alloys under standard baseline processing conditions; varying cooling rates and annealing times to refine lamellar spacing and relieve internal stresses

chosen.conditions: Eutectic high-entropy alloys fabricated by standard procedures, with systematic variations in cooling rates and annealing durations designed to attain a refined eutectic microstructure under ambient and service-relevant temperatures
chosen.why: This approach directly addresses the open question by using a single intervention—tailored thermomechanical processing—to simultaneously enhance strength (through refined lamellar spacing and increased grain boundary/phase interface strengthening) and ductility (via stress relaxation and improved plastic accommodation). Thermal/thermomechanical treatments are well established in materials science, enabling controlled microstructural modifications while providing clear pathways for falsification if the expected improvements in both strength and ductility are not observed relative to the baseline.
